utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. The Prosecution is continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Before I continue my examination-in-chief, if Your Honours please, may I raise an issue that I think needs to be resolved as much as it can be, and that's the procedure of what we do after this witness is finished his examination-in-chief. As you know, it's anticipated that we were going to call Mr. Tihic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- to be the next witness after this witness is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, for cross-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: For cross-examination, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: The issue arises of whether we call him after this witness has been cross-examined or interpose him in between this witness's examination-in-chief and his cross-examination. So in other words, finish this witness, the examination-in-chief of this witness, deal with the cross-examination of Tihic, and then bring this witness back for cross-examination, or rather, keep him here, and then as soon as Mr. Tihic is finished, finish off this witness's cross-examination. Mr. Tihic has recently been appointed to all sorts of new positions in Bosnia and his availability is rapidly becoming problematical, and it is therefore, in the Prosecution's view, imperative that he be dealt with next week and finished next week. So for that reason, I have -- I suggest, and I believe that the Defence have no objection, that we interpose Mr. Tihic, do his cross-examination, and then finish this witness's cross-examination, and then both of them will be finished and can go home, and that would occupy next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The intention being that you -- it's easier to bring Mr. Tihic over the weekend? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, we plan to bring him on the weekend and then start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examine him Monday and complete with him and then he can go and go back? MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. I expect that I'll probably be the rest of the day with Mr. Salkic, and I would dearly love to finish his examination-in-chief today. Whether I do or not, I don't know. But if I didn't, I would probably about only go into a small part of Monday and then the Defence would have Mr. Tihic to cross-examine, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'll hear from the Defence, if any counsel has any objection to interposing Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We have no objection. The joint Defence has no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In the same vein, I would like to remind the parties, especially Mr. Pisarevic, because we had the submission which the Prosecution filed indicating which witnesses had some contacts with Mr. Pisarevic and where the Trial Chamber is of the view that it would be preferable to have the co-counsel cross-examine, and Mr. Tihic is one such witness. So that the cross-examination should be handled by the co-counsel, so the preparations can be done along those lines. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, just one other matter that my co-counsel wanted me to bring up. As you can see, we have been spending a lot of time going over information that hasn't been in these witnesses' statements, and we are just spending a lot of time impeaching. And the problem we are having here is the information that was given to us through discovery, reciprocal discovery, and then also the information which confirmed the indictment, did not include this information. So we sort of feel like - and I'm sure it's no fault of the OTP - but we are feeling a little bit ambushed, or at a disadvantage, rather, because we haven't had a chance to have investigators go out and talk to these witnesses who are part of this new information, investigate, and therefore we have not been able to, we feel, adequately prepare our defence along those lines. So what -- we are just making a specific request right now and just ask for a ruling, whichever way, and whenever the Trial Chamber feels comfortable with giving us a ruling, that if there is new information, newly discovered evidence, or new information we've never heard, that we have a chance to have our investigators check that information out, instead of wasting a lot of time here going back and forth during cross-examination, and then be allowed to recall that witness for a limited purpose, for cross-examination, if need be, on that information. And that's really our only request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For instance, what new information came out of the witness which the Defence had no information previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just brief examples. First of all, with regard to my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic, we faced the situation with the previous witness, Mr. Muhamed Bicic, not saying anything about his presence in this particular event and situation, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean in his previous statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- by the investigators or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And then during his examination-in-chief, a certain description of certain particular situation arose. And then during cross-examination, I tried to establish certain basis. But still, you can understand this is a criminal proceedings. We have to check that on the -- to see maybe eye -- check with the eyewitnesses, you know, so on and so forth. Another example is, for example, yesterday, with regard to the -- I'm speaking on behalf of my colleagues, if you allow me, because of the times. Yesterday, for example -- actually, we don't have this official transcript. That was page 52, lines 15 and then 22 and 25, with regard to Mr. Miroslav Tadic. The particular events related to his presence in front of tank or armed vehicle or something like that, which was not in his previous statements. Another example is related to Mr. Simo Zaric, about the events which were described on page 93, line 9 until 15, with regard to his presence in the corridor of the police building, which was also not mentioned in previous statements. Just as examples. Probably we have more, but we didn't have enough time to elaborate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But the matters you have raised are nothing new in criminal trials. That's nothing new. We've handled such problems before, and it is part of the art of advocacy. It is part of the art of cross-examination. You can challenge a witness whether what he has now said is an afterthought. Whether he has said it because he has heard that this particular person has been arrested, you challenge the witness along those lines. That's the job of cross-examination. The fact that he hasn't mentioned a particular defendant in ten statements prior to the trial does not mean that he should be stopped from mentioning that defendant in Court, and it's your job as Defence counsel to cross-examine and challenge and persuade the Trial Chamber that the fact that he never mentioned this person in ten statements prior to these proceedings means that it's an afterthought and it may not be true. So it's up to you. Very much an advocacy issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You are basically -- I mean, generally you are absolutely right, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. I do see your point when you say that it does not make us -- it does not give you an opportunity to investigate with your witnesses or -- your potential witnesses or your investigators, but that again is a matter for you and your defendant. Because your client tells you where he was, what he was doing, and it is his word, through your cross-examination, against the word of the Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Again, it's a matter of -- your sufficiency in being a Defence counsel. Because if you get instructions from your client he was never near that place. Fine, he was near that place. He never walked along this corridor. That is what you put to the Prosecution witness. It is all art of advocacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You have your instructions. You know what your client says he did, where he was, where he walked, how he dressed, whom he talked to, and that's what you put across in cross-examination. And that's why sometimes when we look at the cross-examination, we wonder what the defence is. Because the places where these people were detained, most of them were public places. A person could have been there for whatever reason. The fact that he was there and he saw a particular person being beaten does not mean he was involved. All those are matters of your art of advocacy, which you can deal with. So it's not a problem that in these ten statements before the trial no mention was -- it's not a problem. It's a matter which actually can afford you ammunition if you know how to deal with a witness when cross-examining. That is why we allow witnesses who are actually discussing the involvement of the accused to be there, in person, in front of the accused, so you can get instructions. Because there is no harm for every Prosecution witness who mentions your client for you to put it to that witness and challenge that evidence, throughout. There is no harm. Because that gives some measure of credibility. If your client comes on the witness box and confirms your cross-examination, all right -- yes, I'm not going to deal with cross-examination in detail, but those are some of the points you deal with. So the fact that my client wasn't mentioned is ammunition for you, assuming that indeed your client was not there. Because it is also a question of credibility between the Prosecution witness, your client, if he decides to give evidence, or his witnesses. So it's really an art of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. But if you allow me just to add a short submission. Assuming the situation where, during the cross-examination - which I agree with you that's an art of advocacy - the Defence were in a situation to have documents, affidavits, eyewitness statements with regard to these particular events. Now, in this particular situation, we have a witness saying something, without previously saying, and then we cannot use all our tools and evidences during the cross-examination of that particular witness. So therefore, I would say it's very focused to the very limited purpose - we shall be very well aware about that - that in some significant and important points, I would say, or events, we would like to have a possibility to additionally cross-examine this witness according to our detailed request filed to the Trial Chamber and your directions and instructions, and then we shall see whether it's worth to have this particular portion of additional cross-examination or not. So I'm not saying that we are going to call 10 or 20 witnesses for re-examination. No, that's not the case. But I'm in general terms speaking about specific moments and issues which will be elaborated between parties in front of this Trial Chamber. So that's the basis of our motion, oral motion, which is actually now, and we kindly ask for the ruling about that motion on this basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain this way: There is nothing wrong to stop the accused, or the Defence counsel for an accused, to recall a Prosecution witness when something new comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was our idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether it is indeed something new or something that should have been expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We are on the same line. Absolutely, we are on the same line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because we are not going to allow recalling witnesses simply because the Defence counsel was not diligent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure you've read the previous decisions of this Tribunal on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. So we are going to establish a basis for that and then wait for the ruling in this specific situation. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I'm sure, if you look at this -- particularly in this case, if you look at the indictment as it is, there are certain paragraphs which make allegations which so far we haven't heard from any witness similarly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A good time for acquittal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And good time for the Prosecution. So we go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, I don't want to prolong this issue any further. I've heard everything that you've said. I understand what the Defence is concerned about, and I fully understand the Trial Chamber's response, with respect, and I entirely agree. However, may I say this to the Defence by way of providing some reassurance: The issue of proofing is complicated. These statements were taken, most of them, in the mid-1990s and the late 1990s. When you get a witness in, you get all sorts of new detail. Occasionally a witness comes up with something that would be a true revelation and something that is apparent to me that would be a matter of obvious interest to the Defence. If that happens, of course, I will undertake to provide the Defence -- inform them of that prior to calling the witness and during the course of my proofing them. So that should go some way to meeting their concerns, and I hope that will provide them with some reassurance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That will be professionally acceptable. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief by Mr. di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, let's return to the events you were describing yesterday. We got to the point where you were being transferred from Brcko to Bijeljina. Can you recall the date that you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were transferred from Brcko to Bijeljina sometime between the 31st and the 1st. I think it was already the 1st of May in the morning, they transferred us to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you started to say yesterday that in the -- on the journey, you were blindfolded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said: As we were departing, some people were blindfolded. However, some took them off later, this way or that way. I think that somebody was given orders not to take them off. So then in a column, one by one, we boarded the bus. There was already over 60 of us, that is to say, that there were new people who were coming in. Among them were people we had not known before, who had not come to Brcko with us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask if the witness could speak into the microphone, come a bit closer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, maybe he could be assisted to sit nearer the microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Move in a bit closer.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you want me to describe this entire journey to Bijeljina now. Is that what you would like, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'll ask you questions, and if you could just give me brief answers. Firstly, what sort of numbers were transferred on the buses? How many people approximately?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was only one bus, and there were over 60 of us, 65 people, or perhaps even more, because at first I did not even know how many people were added to this group of ours that had come from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the majority of people from Bosanski Samac, or were there significant numbers of other prisoners from other areas?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, these were people who were brought from Samac to Brcko. However, we found some detainees who were already there at these barracks and they were added to our group that was going to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the new prisoners who were added to your group?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were also Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they -- the new prisoners who were added to your group, were they combatants? In other words, were they military types or soldiers? Or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found them there in civilian clothes. So based on that assumption, we thought they were civilians. They actually told us that they had been arrested, some of them were taken off a bus in the village of Crkvina near Bosanski Samac, some in the village of Markovic Polje, I think that was the name, yet others in the town of Brcko itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the prisoners on that bus suffer from any form of mental handicap or psychiatric disorder?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were joined there by a young man who was about 24 or 25 years old, certainly not more than that, and he must have been retarded. We actually heard them saying, "What do we do with him?" And then they said that they would put him on the bus too, and then he went to Bijeljina together with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was escorting you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was escorting us, and their vehicles -- the bus was a civilian bus, but the vehicles that were escorting us were vehicles with JNA markings on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn your attention now to your arrival in Bijeljina, please. Where in Bijeljina were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken to the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the young man who was mentally handicapped?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll have to give you a broader description concerning that. I can't do this briefly. We were going out one by one. Our hands were on our heads. Among us was this young man who was mentally retarded. They took him to the other side, and they said something to the effect of, "What do we do with him?" They took him about 15 or 20 metres away from us, and then we would go along the same path later. Then I heard shots, as people say, bursts of gunfire. So he was shot at. A minute or two later, we had to pass that same way to the rooms where they would detain us. We saw this young man lying in blood. I'm sure he was dead. Oh, yes. Before that, he said that they beat him as they were taking him away and that they were saying that he is the one who allegedly raped Serb children, something like that. And I doubt that this young man could have done a thing like that, but that's what I heard, so it's not for me to say whether he actually did it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got any insight into the ethnic background of this young man?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know. When they were boarding him, somebody addressed him by his name. I'm sure he was a Muslim, but believe me, I can't remember his actual name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you taken into cells?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These weren't cells. First they took us upstairs to some classrooms and they -- I don't know. The windows were probably too big or something. So they took us from one classroom to another and ultimately we ended up at the gym that was within the barracks compound. So that's where they put us in. And when I say "put us in," I mean that they kicked us, hit us with rifle butts. This was a kind of welcome they accorded us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you were transferred there on the 31st [sic] of April or the 1st of May. How long did you remain in Bijeljina in all?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijeljina, we stayed there until the 13th of May, the 13th of May. On the 13th of May, we were transferred back to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to ask you some questions about your stay in Bijeljina. Do you know someone nicknamed Pekar, or "the Baker"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone nicknamed Brico, or "the Barber"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you meet those people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not meet them in a good context either. These were two soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army. I don't know their actual names. One of them was addressed as Pekar and the other one as Brico. They got into the gym. They started calling us Ustasha or balija motherfuckers, Zengas, whatever. They ordered us to line up along the wall, facing the walls, and then we were supposed to kneel and remain kneeling. That was very difficult. However, that wasn't the end of that. They went from one person to the other and they kicked us in the back, in the area where our kidneys are, with their army boots. Many of us were badly hurt, myself included. For a few days, I could not move at all. When they would practically carry me to the toilet, because I could not walk, my legs were numb. I could not urinate normally. I only urinated blood. So we were being beaten and all of that. This was quite a misfortune. And a gentleman who was addressed as Nikolic came, and then he managed to stop some of this. Until this gentleman came -- I think he was a lieutenant or a first class lieutenant or something like that, but I remember his name was Nikolic. Hadzialijagic, Safet who was there, he was also in trouble and he had heart problems and every blow was a risk to his life. Many, many people were beaten badly there until Mr. Nikolic came. MR. DI FAZIO: Would the Chamber just bear with me for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this fellow Nikolic's first name? Have you got any idea what it was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name was Milan, or something similar, but I do remember the surname, because for us, it meant an improvement. And so if anything was a bit better, you would remember it under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it the case that after his intervention, you and the other prisoners were no longer beaten? Is that a correct assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not 100 per cent, but I would say yes, because some people did still manage to come in. But luckily for us, once again, a day or two later, this same man, Nikolic, came and saw us in an even worse state, and he immediately called the guards and told them that nobody was allowed to come inside any more, because he said, "We are not here to decide who is guilty and who isn't, who did what." And he sort of placed a veto on their coming into our room, and should anybody come to beat us, then the guard could not prevent us from calling him. And actually this happened in one of the days that followed. Whether it was the next day or not, I'm not quite sure. But once again this Brico, "the Barber," and Pekar, "the Baker," came in and started beating us, and Mr. Nikolic came by and stood in the doorway, and we considered him to be our saviour already because at least when he was there, we felt safe. As I say, when he came there, he said something to them, he said, "Why are you beating those people? If you want to beat somebody, then go to Vukovar or the front line or something like that and take some prisoners of your own and then do that to them, the same thing that you're doing to these people here." He would say something along those lines or he would say, "Well, let me pick one of them out and give you an even fight. Because it is not an even fight if somebody has to kneel down for you to be able to beat them." So that's what he would do. He would bring in a doctor, too. We had regular food; it was sufficient. And so it was quite a bit better when he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were Lukac, Tihic, [redacted] still in custody in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever leave Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can describe that detail for you. One day - I can't remember the exact date - they came and called out Mr. Tihic, Lukac, Grga Zubak, Sead Mujkanovic, the late uncle Franjo, I think his surname was Barukcic, and another one, another man whom we didn't know, who was added on to us. In fact, they brought in several people whom we didn't know. So I'm not sure of his name. But we heard before they had come to fetch them, by the noise and sounds going on outside, that a helicopter had landed at the barracks. And at one particular moment, a young man turned up at the door. I was lying down because I was in a very bad state. I was almost unable to move. But I saw him standing in the doorway. He was wearing a pilot uniform, a pilot's overall, and the people told me later that he was a young guy from Samac who was a pilot at Batajnica airport in Belgrade or something of that kind, and that he had brought them a box of biscuits, and they managed to learn that they were taking these gentlemen off somewhere further, to Belgrade, to Batajnica, something like that. They left, and I didn't see them there again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the pilot's name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a young guy, younger than me. I know his parents because they lived in Samac, but I think his surname was Ninkovic or something similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you -- you said that people later told you he was from Samac. Did you have any independent knowledge, your own knowledge, that he was from Samac, or was it the case that you were told that he was from Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I failed to mention this, but I think I did: I knew the man from before, when he was a boy and when he went to school, so I already knew him. Nobody had to tell me that it was him. But from the other people there, I heard that he had told them that he was taking them but that this should be a secret, that they shouldn't divulge that to anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn now to your transfer out of Bijeljina back to Bosanski Samac. How were you transported from Bijeljina back to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on that 13th of May - and I remember that date because it was police day, or militia day, as it was known at the time - we were transported by bus to Samac, to the gym hall of the secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you this: Was it all of the -- apart from the fellows who departed on the helicopter for Serbia, was it the entirety of the Bosanski Samac prisoners who were transferred to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except we would always get some new ones in who were added on to us. So not the same numbers went back, apart from the ones who left by helicopter. Some other new additions, new arrivals, were brought in and -- brought into the same camp that we were in. So there were new additions to us. I can remember some of their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of numbers are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say the new people, four, five, six perhaps. Some of the names I remember very well, even to this day, so that I know that there were two brothers, Croats, from Derventa, for example. There were two young guys from Modrica, Tarevac, and a few others. I also know that some people stayed on after we had left: a Muslim, Kapetan, and some officers. I don't know what happened to them, what their fate was. I never heard anything. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown photograph F48 from Exhibit P14A, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Three buildings are depicted in that photograph. Please identify the one that's in the foreground on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the gym hall belonging to the secondary school centre, shown from the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at it from the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now go to the destroyed building on the left-hand side of the photograph, also in the foreground, and point to it and tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say on the right-hand side? I think you said the right, whereas this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I did. I meant the left. If I did say the right, I apologise. I meant the left-hand side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to avoid misunderstanding, I had to correct you there on that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you, Mr. Salkic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is the gym hall of the secondary school centre, and these are the premises of the primary school and this is the gym hall belonging to the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be absolutely clear, the one in the foreground on the left-hand side of the photograph with the wrecked roof is the primary school, and the one in the distance --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that you can see in between the two buildings is the gym of the primary school? Is that a correct --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were taken from Bijeljina to Bosanski Samac, where were you initially imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was here, in this building. That's the gym hall belonging to the secondary school centre. But we passed by this way, and all this went on the other side. The yard of the secondary school centre and the entrance to the gym hall was the other side as well. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks. I've finished with the photograph, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe to the Chamber your reception at this high school gym.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll describe that in detail for you. As you can see, on the basis of what I have said so far, there were frequent changes. So we were always ready to see what they had in store for us next, and you have heard what they usually had in store for us. But anyway, the bus parked in the yard not far from the entrance door, 8 to 10 metres from where we were to go in. And they were already drunk, and the policemen said they were celebrating, it was their day, they should be resting, and why did we have to come to upset this. And they made a gauntlet and beat us as we ran through this gauntlet with our hands up behind our necks. We actually had to run to avoid being beaten. And we went into the gym hall one by one. Later on they came in after us and lined us up around the walls, and once again the welcoming ceremony: songs, beatings, blows, swearing and cursing of our balija and Ustasha mothers. That was their welcome package in the first half hour or hour after our arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple of quick questions that arise from your answer. What time of day was this? Was it in the morning or the afternoon or the evening?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the afternoon. I think it was between 2.00, half past 2.00, 3.00, 4.00. You lost track of time in situations like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. You've also commented that the policemen said that it was their day. Is there any significance in that, it being their day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said. It was police day that was celebrated in the former Yugoslavia on that date. It was the date and day when the police force celebrated its day. That's in simple terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you knew any of the people who were conducting the beatings as you ran through the gauntlet? In other words, give us names, if you know of any names.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we met some of them while we were in Samac briefly, and I was later to learn some of the other names during the time I spent there. So actually, I could tell you quite a lot of names. Here's an example: Sole, Zvaka, Rakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you before you continue to identify, as you give us a name, to identify whether you knew this person -- that person to be a Serb from Serbia or whether that person was a local. That's what I'm interested in finding out. So names and whether they were local or not. Okay?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular moment when we arrived, the people who were there, almost all of them -- not almost all of them, but certainly all of them were locals, local Serbs. And later we would learn who Rakic was, that he was from Novi Grad, that Zvaka was from Karic, and all the others. Some of them we already knew from before. I knew where they were from. But they were local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the men who formed the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and who beat us too. And all of them were active. I didn't notice a single one who was not active in giving us this welcome. And when I say "active," I mean beating us. So all of them beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the high school gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't stay there long. Two or three days. I'm not quite sure, but I think that it was on the third day -- rather, on the fourth day we were transported further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to the gym hall belonging to the primary school, which was the building that I indicated on the photograph you showed me a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we get there, though, I want to ask you a few more questions about events in the high school gym. You've described that you were beaten when you first arrived and that you had to sing songs once you had been taken inside. In the period of time that you were in the high school gym, for those three or four days, were you beaten again?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was non-stop, all the time. There was this singing. You had to stand there. They came in and beat you and beat you and then said, "Come on. Sing the songs." And they were the Chetnik songs that I had already said. There weren't any other songs. They just told us to sing those particular songs. You had to stand, sing. Your throat would dry up, your voice would go, people would fall down unconscious. They were terrible things that were happening there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period of time that you were in the high school gym, did you see any of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That last day, when we were to be transported to the gym hall of the primary school. At the doorway, Mr. Todorovic turned up, in the presence of Mr. Blagoje Simic, who is here -- who was there, not far. He didn't come into the gym hall, but he was standing in the doorway, actually. And when somebody comes in, there would be general silence. The first thing that I thought of, that came into my head, knowing that he was a functionary, I thought: Well, maybe there will be an exchange of some kind or maybe some of us would be released. Perhaps our troubles have come to an end. But unfortunately, all he did was - and I'm going to quote him - he said, "Ooph." And he addressed Mr. Todorovic, and he sighed, "Ooph, there's a lot of space still here," and made no further comment. They left. We didn't know what this meant, what he meant by that, but at least we were happy that Todorovic hadn't beat us. And the gentleman didn't beat me, so I wasn't afraid of him, because I assumed that he wouldn't stoop to that level like the others. But they left. We were happy and commented, discussed, what this could mean, but we didn't even imagine what would happen until the following morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the company of Todorovic, were there any other men who were with the both of them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some guys in uniform standing behind them, but they didn't come into the hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you were taken from the high school gym to the primary school gym after three or four days.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly tell us how you made it from one place to the other.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the buildings are close by, only 60 to 70 metres apart, we went there on foot, one by one. We walked. Of course, there were some guards, armed guards providing security to ensure that nobody escaped, but we crossed this space one by one, in a column, and went to the primary school gym --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that's where we were put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that mean that the high school gym no longer served any purpose?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was empty after we had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it ever filled again?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- who filled it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day -- and we realised then why Mr. Simic had sighed and said, "Ooph, there is a lot of room still here." Anyway, they took us to the neighbouring building attached to the primary school, and that day they began to bring in new people, and we were able - and I can show this on the photograph that was here a moment ago - we were able to see what was happening. Croats were being brought in groups of two, three, five, fifteen, I don't know in which order. But as we knew the people, from the distance we were at, we were able to see them quite well, and we would say, "Oh, there goes so and so," or, "There goes that other man."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we saw that it was all clear, pure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the ethnic background of these groups of -- small groups of men who were being taken to the high school gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I said what I said. They were only Croats, just Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us if -- you recognised them. Does mean that they were locals?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some locals, some elderly people, 60 years old, 70 years old, some young ones too. All sorts, different ages. But we recognised uncle Mato Rukavina -- no, that wasn't the name. It was my wife's brother's father. He was 67, 68. I know that he was ill. So it didn't matter to them what you were. All they were concerned about was that you didn't belong to their ethnicity and that you were brought in, hauled in, if you weren't the same as them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in the primary school gym from the time we were transferred, which was, let's say, the 17th or 15th, 16th, of May, when we were transferred there, until the middle of September, the latter half of September. I can't tell you the exact date, but the second half of September. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I want to show the witness a number of photographs. Can the usher please prepare photographs 48, 49, 57, 58, 59, 64, and 66. Perhaps if we deal first with 48 -- I'm sorry, 49.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the baton, please identify which is the primary school and which is the primary school gym.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What building? What is it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the gym hall belonging to the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other one, the other building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this building here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is another building that was destroyed. It's not here any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you could see the high school gym being filled up with small groups of Croats, local Croats, and you could see this from the primary school gym. Can you point to where in the building you had this vantage point, from what window you could see the high school gym? Or is it not depicted in the photo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is depicted, and I can show it to you. All the windows here that was fairly high up, underneath them, there were what we called the Swedish ladders, the general type of thing you would find in a gym hall. This was where the door was and steps. So this was no longer used as an exit, although the door stayed on. So from there, you could see across the school yard, and you could see very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 57, please. That appears to be the interior of a ruined building. What building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a corridor in front of the entrance. This was the door, the entrance into the gym, the primary school gym, and this was a small anteroom. Now, there is a wall missing here. That's where the wall was, which doesn't exist any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have not asked you, but can you tell us where you were actually kept, which room you were actually kept in, during the period of time that you were in the primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would pass this hallway and go through this main entrance. This was the main entrance into the gym. So we were inside, in the gym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And look at F58, please. What's that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance door leading into the hallway, and then on the left, you go to the gym, and to the right, you go to the classrooms of the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And F59, please? What does -- what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the gym itself very well here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the room in which the prisoners were incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in that room, somewhere around here, a bit further this side. That particular corner is missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were there, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where I was detained, incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. I understand that you were incarcerated in that room, but you pointed to a specific spot. What did you mean when you pointed to that specific spot and said, "I was here"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the spot where I was, where I was lying. Now, this is really a good opportunity. Let me explain something else. Look at the floor, the tiles. That's where we slept all the time, without a blanket, without anything underneath us, that is to say, on plain tiles, in the T-shirts that we were brought in. So -- see? There weren't any beds there or blankets or anything, just plain tiles, and we slept on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about bits of cardboard or paper or something like that? Did you have that at least?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If - if - somebody managed to find something like that, with the exception of a few people who managed to do that, of course, like in any gym, there were - what do you call them - gym mats, but they took them away from us afterwards. They said that that was too comfortable, too soft, even when people managed to get hold of these gym mats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's 11.00. It's actually past 11.00. I was just trying to see if we could finish the photographs. We will take our break and resume our proceedings at 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. We were looking at photograph number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO: We were looking at photograph number F59.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the distance is a -- and in the centre of the photograph, in the far distance of the room, is a window that goes almost down to ground level. Is that the window through which you could see the Croat men being led into the high school gym, or was that some other window or some other vantage point?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's not a window; it's a door. This part here that I'm going to show, that's a door. It's a big double door with glass on it so you could see very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But is that the window -- or is that the door or the point through which you looked to see the Croat men being led in dribs and drabs into the high school building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at 64 now, please, F64 of Exhibit P14A. On the right is depicted a darkened doorway, presumably leading into some other room. If you walk through that doorway into that darkened room that you can see on the right-hand side of the photograph, where would that take you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll show that to you. It's the door over here. That leads to the gym. But over here there was a wall previously. That's the wall that's missing, the one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just take note, if you can, of the open window that you can see in F64, looking out apparently onto open ground. Okay? Can you now be shown F66. Can you see the open window that was depicted in F64 in F66?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can show that. It's the window over here, with a view from the yard of the school. That's the window that you asked me to remember a few minutes ago. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. May I ask the usher's assistance in providing a further exhibit to the witness, P30 ter. It's the map that was created by Mr. Zecevic. And if the photographs could be left there, because I'll be using them in conjunction with P30 ter. May I also provide the usher with a clean copy of P30 ter? It's both the English and in the B/C/S. The B/C/S is the second page. It's identical. Just keep that P30 and also the new clean copy. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the photograph F59, please. Can you see, Mr. Salkic, that it's looking in a particular direction, that photograph?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to take the P30 ter now and draw an arrow depicting the direction in which the -- MR. DI FAZIO: I've got a smaller pen, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you just draw an arrow quickly on the photograph and show us the direction on the map that the camera is looking in, in 59?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the entrance door. So that's the view over here, viewed inside, I mean. Just a minute. I have an objection. Just a minute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, place it on the ELMO so that we can see what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, this door is not here. It's here. So this door was not put in the right place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I went in there an endless number of times, when I went to primary school, when I went to do sports. I passed there over a thousand times. I know exactly where it is. And that's when I explained this to you that the wall was missing. So the door is not over here the way the gentleman had drawn it, but it is on the other side, over here. So from here, you have a view of the gym itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just put the number "59" next to that little arrow that you've drawn there so that we know that that's the direction in which photograph 59 is looking, please? Just near it in small numbers, near the arrow that you drew, near the arrow that you drew. Okay. Thanks. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I'm wondering whether that "59" is on the correct spot. You were telling him to put the "59" on the arrow which the witness drew. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. He drew two arrows, and I repeated it twice, but that's where he put the "59." We've heard his evidence. We've heard his evidence that that's the general direction that the way the camera is looking, except he says that door was a bit over to the side. So I don't think it will matter -- amount to much, that discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. di Fazio, should that have been drawn on the clean copy? Because it looks as though it's been drawn on the actual exhibit and not on the clean copy that you gave to the usher. MR. DI FAZIO: I thought it was drawn on the clean copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I don't think it is. If you look in the right-hand corner, it says the exhibit number or whatever, ter. MR. DI FAZIO: May I approach the witness and have a look?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Make sure he does it on the clean copy and then we can have a number for the clean copy. MR. DI FAZIO: No, it's not on the exhibit, if Your Honour pleases. You'll see that the exhibit label is on the back of the document that the usher is holding. So that was written in, but I think it's handwriting of one of the counsel. So this will be created as a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So can we have a number for the clean copy, please? Not the clean copy, the one that the witness has marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P30/1. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, can you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ter, sorry. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Now, can we just go to photograph F64? Place that briefly on the ELMO so we can all remind ourselves what it depicts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that photograph, Mr. Salkic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the same map that you've marked, can you indicate with an arrow -- on the same map that you have already marked, can you indicate with an arrow the direction that that particular photograph is, for want of a better expression, looking in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Near that little arrow, can you put the number "F64," please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. All right. F57 now? Could you just show -- if the usher could just show us that particular photograph, F57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, please take note of that photograph. Do you see it? Thank you. Now, can you repeat the exercise with an arrow on the same document? Can you show us in which direction that particular photograph is looking and then place the arrow on the page.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And put the "F57" next to that.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks. And finally, F58. I don't think my learned friends will dispute that that's the entrance, and you can see that marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us again with an arrow which way the photograph is looking?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And don't forget the number, "F58."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: I've finished with the photos and that map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you questions now about the conditions in the primary school gym. First of all, I want to ask you about any beatings that you or other prisoners received, and I'm asking you to provide a general picture of what the situation was in respect of beatings during the period of time that you were there. Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that gym, we spent many a day. All of us who were detained here, we would agree that it was hell. We were beaten every day. Whoever wanted to come, came whenever they wanted to come. They beat us in every conceivable way. It was not restricted in terms of time either. Morning, afternoon, evening, people came whenever they wanted to, whenever it came to their minds. This was such torture. Within one day -- and when I say "a day," I'm referring to 24 hours - it felt like 140 hours to us. They would come in groups, different groups. They would beat us. They would beat us up really badly. It was hell, to put it simply. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In addition to all of that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that they were satisfied with the beatings only. They made us sing until we would fall, and when I say "singing," I mean those Chetnik songs again. We would have to stand, all beaten up, starving, because the food was horrible. As a matter of fact, it was no good whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This period was hell, real hell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take you back and just ask you a few more questions about the beatings. Did they use instruments?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They would bring some with them; some they had there, because there was a makeshift workshop there. Because there was a janitor there who was involved in the maintenance of the school building, so there were rods, metal sticks, wooden sticks. Some they would bring with them. And sometimes we would even joke among ourselves. When they would bring truncheons, we would joke amongst ourselves and say, "Oh, good. A banana only." It hurt less. At least it didn't break our bodies. So there were different objects there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- iron objects, other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that whoever wanted to come, came whenever they wanted to. Who were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody. Serbs, civilians came, even some women came to beat us, soldiers, policemen. Whenever people wanted to come, the door would simply open and they would walk in, they would beat us. That was the impression you'd have there: Whoever wanted to, came. There was a man called Pero Pita - that's what we called him - in Samac. He was a retard. And we were expecting him to come any day, but I guess he was smarter than everybody else and he would not stoop that low to come to beat us too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that civilians came, do you mean local civilians?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They would come in soldier uniforms, in police uniforms, sometimes civilians too. So in fact, it was open season. This was probably some kind of fun for them. Instead of going out to jog, they came to beat us, and they would take it out on us by beating us and making us sing Chetnik songs, and also starving us, because it was really horrible. After such beatings, after 24 hours, you would get a little slice of bread with a tiny little bit of marmalade on it - not a big spoon of marmalade, no - and possibly a cup of tea. Often, as a matter of fact, instead of marmalade, they would bring us lard. And then they tried to insult us that way. I didn't mind. I have always eaten pork. I eat pork nowadays as well. But they would say, "Balijas, Muslims, here you go, pork," not only lamb and other kinds of meat. So it was that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not troubled by any edict against eating pork or pork products, but were any of you other Muslim prisoners troubled by that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were people that wouldn't eat that. They didn't want to eat that. They would just eat the bread. But to tell you quite honestly, I ate it before that and after that. It bothered me, but what? I had to survive. As a matter of fact, I thought that it would be good for me because it would give me more calories so I could survive. It's the logic that we had to apply, because they made us do that, even these people who would not do that because their religious customs would not allow that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Slavko Trivunovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nicknamed Zubar, "the Dentist."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he acquire that nickname?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got that nickname from us, the prisoners, because, unfortunately, other people had bad experience with him and that nickname of his. I personally didn't. Should I describe this case to the Trial Chamber? You will tell me whether I should or whether I shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber, firstly, of what his activities were and, secondly, why you weren't troubled by him.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: He was a Serb policeman. His role was to guard us there so that no one would escape or something like that. And he beat us. At first he beat me too. However, when I found out that he was Trivunovic, and I knew his uncle Ignjo Trivunovic, who was from the village of Obudovac. Branica is the name of the part of the village that he came from. I was fed up, so I took advantage of one opportunity and I said, "Trivunovic, my goodness, go and ask your uncle what kind of a person I am, and if I'm a bad person, he can tell you that and then you can come here and kill me if you want. I won't mind." I was guided by the following. While I worked at the Utva company, this uncle of his was supposed to be fired, and it was not his fault. The company had sued him and taken him to court. However, he knew that, in that particular case, I was there on the ground and I knew what was true and what was not true. And he asked me if I wanted to be a witness for him, and I said yes. But then other problems came up. I was defending a man who was being sued by the company, and then the people from the company said to me that if I were to testify in his behalf, that I could easily share his fate, that is to say, be fired. Nevertheless, I decided to testify for this gentleman, Mr. Trivunovic, and he was quite appreciative of that. Soon after that, I left the firm of my own accord and I started up my own business, and he remained quite grateful to me. So then when this gentleman went to see his uncle and when talked to him, he sent through him a little parcel to me, like a sandwich. He thanked me and he had said to him that I was a very good and honest man. So from then onwards, Slavko never beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm interested in what he did to others. Can you tell us -- provide us with details of his activities with respect to other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others received the same treatment, like I did before this particular event when we talked. He continued to beat the others, just like Jacimovic did, who called himself a Serb inspector. So he continued doing the same thing that he had been doing, until that particular moment, to me as well. In a way, I was spared by him. However, I don't know if I should tell you about this. A very unfortunate incident occurred during the night. When he entered through the door, I saw him quite well in the moonlight. Also this was summertime, and I recognised his voice. He was wearing white clogs, some kind of a white T-shirt. He opened the door to the gym that I showed you a few minutes ago. He was looking for a volunteer. This had been going on for some 10 or 15 days; he hadn't been beating me, that is. And then I, perhaps in order to protect others, I said, "Slavko, what do you need? Here I am." And then he said that I could sit down, that he didn't need me. At that moment, other people walked in wearing uniforms, police uniforms, army uniforms, and all hell broke loose. Beatings. Slavko and other people started taking the men out. The first one that got out was Mr. Dragan Delic and then Safet Hadzialijagic. That's because they were right by the door. And then one after the other. I was skipped. I can still remember quite a few names. They were taken out one by one. Their teeth were being pulled out, five, seven, two, three, whatever. However, we found all of that out later. Although we heard moans and screams, it never crossed our mind that they could think of such a stupid thing to do. I don't know what else to call it. I mean, why would a person come and pull out five or six or seven teeth? That's what we found out after this rite was performed. This went on for perhaps an hour or an hour and a half, and that is how Mr. Slavko Trivunovic got this nickname, Zubar, "the Dentist."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall when, during the period of time that you were imprisoned in the primary school gym, that this incident occurred? Was it towards the end of the period of time, around the middle of the time you were there, the beginning? And if you can be precise, do tell us, but I'm trying to get a fix on what time, what period of the year this was.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are not getting translation. And the witness just has to start the answer again because there was no interpretation at all. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Salkic, unfortunately we just didn't get your answer. Do tell us, I'm sorry, but can you please repeat what you just said?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were speaking about the period this happened. You were asking me when this happened. It was towards the end of June, or perhaps it was July. I think that it was actually the beginning of July, and perhaps it went on until mid-July. Perhaps it went on until later as well. I think it was the end of July, actually, or mid-August even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But quite certainly it did happen, and all those sitting on the left-hand side know that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, are you familiar with a game called Russian roulette?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see that game played [Microphone not activated] at the primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, yes. You said "game," and it was called Russian roulette. But it was no game, let me tell you. It was a matter of life or death. And, yes, it did take place before my very eyes. Unfortunately, you were there waiting, waiting to hear the shot go off. And our colleague, the man who was with me, unfortunately we found him dead on this occasion. I don't know whether you want me to explain that game, how it was played, and in whose presence. If so, please tell me. Do you want me to go ahead and describe it or not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I -- I'm not quite sure what you mean by the expression "our colleague, the man who was with you, and who was unfortunately found dead." I just don't follow that. Can you explain what you meant, before you tell us about the episode.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I apologise. And perhaps the interpretation wasn't the right one. I said thank goodness that nobody was killed, that nobody was found dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to describe the events that you witnessed in the primary school gym.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Todorovic turned up, Goran Ristic as well. Goran, I think that his surname was Hasic, this other man's, and some other people too. And the beatings started again. Stevan Todorovic, with the exception of one time when he came to the secondary school accompanied by Mr. Blagoje Simic, that was the only time that he didn't beat us; otherwise, all the other times that he came visiting, there were beatings. So it was only when he turned up with Mr. Blagoje that he didn't beat us. As I say, they started beating us, breaking our bones, and then there was a lull, and they said, "Let my Ustashas come out." And we knew that he always liked to refer to the Ustashas, and as he said, he would always give them a portion of the beatings. They would receive their regular portion. And they were two brothers from Vidovice, Markovic Polje, who joined us in all of our travels. And there were two brothers, also Croats, who were from Derventa. There was a man called Behrem, Masic and others. There was Mesic, Masic, I think there was a similar surname of this other person as well. And he would first of all take the two brothers out. I don't want to give their names because of the developments that I am going to recount later on, unless the Trial Chamber insists. But there will be some personal unpleasantness, so if I could be spared from saying their names. So please tell me, do I have to state their names or not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you don't. And, Mr. Salkic, I'm asking you now about the game of Russian roulette. Okay? I'm not asking you about anything else. I just want you to confine your comments to the game of Russian roulette that you observed, all right? So please continue and describe what you saw.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the brothers, the Croats. But as I don't want to say their names, I will continue describing the events. And it is because of the subsequent events that I don't want to state their names. I'm going to have to say some ugly things, and then you could link up the two brothers from Derventa and others, and their names would become public in that way. MR. DI FAZIO: Just pause. If Your Honours please, given what the witness has said, it might be advisable at this stage to go into private session. This episode that I am eliciting evidence of is not a matter that requires private session at all, there's nothing in it whatsoever that would require any sort of private session, and the witness has been warned by me not to mention names. However - and I have no reason for thinking this at all - but given what he has just said now for the first time, it might be advisable to go into private session to avoid public transmission of other events that might concern some of the people he's going to talk about, and by that I mean matters of sexual misconduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I can't say that this evidence has got anything to do with that, but -- and I have no reason to think that it will necessarily lead into that, but there is that risk, and for that reason I think it would be advisable if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We do have a duty to protect witnesses' integrity and other persons mentioned. Only for those purposes, we can go into private session. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you. It's only going to be for a few minutes. This evidence won't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed. We are now in open session. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I'd like to ask you if, in the period of time that you were in the primary school gym, whether any of the defendants attended there, went there.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- withdraw that question. Can you recall approximately when he turned up?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the day and month, or the time of day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have made that clearer. I'm talking about the time of year. About when in the time that you were imprisoned did he turn up, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. I understand your question now. It happened in mid-June, give or take a few days. I can't quite specify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time of the day did he appear?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was night-time. It was already dark. Between 9.30 and 10.00, half past 10.00 at the latest. Perhaps even later. We weren't able to know what the exact time was because we didn't have watches, but judging by when it got dark, and we knew what season it was, it was dark at 9.00, and so much time had elapsed, so that was the orientation. We didn't have watches, so I can't be specific in terms of time, the exact minute and hour, but he came at night, at about 10.00 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned on one or two occasions that the primary school gym was dark. Was it ever lit or provided with any sort of lighting, artificial light?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes. A flashlight and the moonlight that filtered through. As the windows were high up on the walls, you could see fairly well -- well, not well, but you could make out what you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that he arrived. It was in the evening. It was dark -- night-time, I should say. Was he in company with anyone?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were others with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately how many men were with him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About five or six. If you want me to, I can describe his appearance and the sequence of events when he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly I'll be asking you about that, but let me just ask you a few questions first. You presumably were inside the gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he enter the gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the men with him enter the gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the men were wearing, Mr. Simic himself and the men who accompanied him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people wearing uniforms. They were armed. They were wearing uniforms, yes, and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the men when Milan Simic first entered the gym? When I say that, "men," I mean the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the door opened, late at night, we knew that this would be a visit which would result in the same thing it always did. We would have to jump up, stand to attention, and wait to see what was in store for us. And that's what happened on that occasion, too. The door opened, Mr. Simic came in, with his escorts, as he said. I don't know whether that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we should get up and stand at attention and did we know that it was a Serb minister who was entering the room and do we know who he is. Many of us recognised his voice. He even introduced himself to us as Milan Simic, the Serb minister, and other things like that. And then things went the way they went. So he said to us that he was this Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he provide any explanation as to why he was there or say anything that gave any clue as to why he was there?
